title: "Limitations"

aliases:

toc-depth: 2
---

OPDI is built from the position reports that the OpenSky Network's receivers
pick up: where no receiver hears an aircraft, nothing can be computed, and
most limits come from that. A found event can still be wrong; a missing one
says nothing about what the aircraft did
([found is not the same as correct](accuracy/index.qmd#two-measures-availability-and-accuracy)).

- How each item is computed: [OPDI Algorithms](algorithms/index.qmd).
- How often it exists and how close it is to the records: [Data quality](accuracy/index.qmd).
- Each item's figures at the 100 busiest airports in Europe and worldwide: [Airports](accuracy/airports.qmd#lookup).
- The shares and times below are over the [three days measured](accuracy/index.qmd#the-three-days).

## Summary

| Item | Main limits | Where it is reliable |
|---|---|---|
| [Tracks](#lim-tracks) (`flight_id`) | Can hold part of a flight; circuits with full stops at one airport stay one row; placeholder addresses merge aircraft. | Airliners with continuous reception and a call sign per flight. |
| [Airports](#lim-airports) (`adep`, `ades`) | Small airfields and heliports never named; arrivals lost far out get no destination. | Medium and large airports; source `runway_event`. |
| [Aircraft details](#lim-aircraft) | Database of October 2024; no type for about one flight in six. | Airliners registered before late 2024. |
| [First and last seen](#lim-first-last-seen) (`first_seen`, `last_seen`) | Describe reception, not the flight. | Everywhere, as reception times. |
| [Milestone columns](#lim-flight-list-milestones) | As available as their events; one take-off and one landing per row. | Where their events are reliable. |
| [Take-off and landing](#lim-take-off-landing) (`ATOT`, `ALDT`) | Need reception near the runway; runway-window times (`legacy`) less precise. | Reception down to the runway; `info.method` = `acdm`. |
| [Other runway events](#lim-runway) (`line-up`, `take-off-roll`, `xing-runway-threshold`, `runway-vacated`, `go-around`, `runway-crossing-entry`, `runway-crossing-vacated`) | Need reports on the runway; at the first or last report when reception starts or ends there. | Ground reception on the runways. |
| [Block times](#lim-block-times) (`AOBT`, `AIBT`) | Need reception at the stand before the aircraft leaves it; off-block late when first received on a taxiway. | Dense ground reception and named stands in OpenStreetMap; `info.first_seen_on` = `stand` or `apron`. |
| [Airport surface](#lim-surface) (`entry-{element}`, `exit-{element}`) | Need ground reception and a mapped layout; vehicles carry transponders. | Large airports with good ground reception and a detailed map. |
| [Vertical profile](#lim-vertical) (`top-of-climb`, `top-of-descent`, `level-start`, `level-end`, `level-off-climb-start`, `level-off-climb-end`, `level-off-descent-start`, `level-off-descent-end`, `xing-fl{level}`) | Not validated; slow aircraft and tracks cut by reception give odd profiles. | Jet airliners with a cruise; tops with `info.observed` true (not at the edge of reception). |
| [Distance circles](#lim-rings) (`xing-{radius}nm`) | Only around the row's two airports; position steps near spoofing. | 40 and 100 NM circles with good reception around them. |
| [Flight information region (FIR) crossings](#lim-fir) (`xing-fir`) | One AIRAC cycle for every day. | Lateral crossings in airspace with continuous reception. |
| [Holding](#lim-holding) (`holding-start`, `holding-end`) | Circling for other reasons meets the definition. | Holds with `info.context` = `arrival`. |
| [Point merge](#lim-point-merge) (`pms-leg-entry`, `pms-leg-exit`, `pms-merge-point`) | Only the airports in the reference table. | Airports in the table with good reception on the arcs. |
| [Measurements](#lim-measurements) (`distance_flown_nm`, `time_passed_s`) | Count from the start of the track, not of the flight. | Differences between two events of a flight. |

## General limits {#general-limits}

### ADS-B reception {#ads-b-reception}

Everything in OPDI comes from **ADS-B** (Automatic Dependent
Surveillance–Broadcast): radio messages in which an aircraft broadcasts its
position, altitude and speed. The OpenSky receivers, run by volunteers and
institutions, are on the ground, unevenly spread, and hear aircraft in line
of sight: a few hundred kilometres away at cruise altitude, only close by
near the ground.

- No receiver near, no data: often over oceans, deserts and other areas with
  few receivers, and on the ground at many airports.
- Cruise events are found almost everywhere, runway events at fewer
  airports, stand events at fewer still. A missing block time, runway event
  or surface event mostly means the surface was not heard, not that nothing
  happened ([airports where ground events are nearly absent](accuracy/airports.qmd#ground-reception)).
- Aircraft without ADS-B, or not broadcasting it, are not in the data.
- ADS-C reports, sent by satellite mainly over the oceans, are not used,
  so the ocean gaps stay.
- Counts from OPDI (flights per airport, movements per runway) are lower
  bounds, not totals. The share of an airport's traffic OPDI sees varies by
  airport and by day ([OPDI Sensors: where next](sensors-expansion.qmd)
  measures it over European airports in 2025).

### Flights are tracks

OPDI uses no flight plans. A **flight** is a **track**: the position reports
of one aircraft that belong together ([Track identity](algorithms/tracks.qmd)),
from where reception starts to where it ends. A track that holds several
flights is divided, and the flight list has one row per flight.

- Every track has a row in the flight list, with no minimum duration.
  Departure and destination airports come from the track and are empty when
  it begins or ends away from an airport; a track with no airport has both
  empty ([Departure and destination airports](algorithms/airports.qmd)).
  A very short track is often a piece of a flight whose other pieces are
  on other rows (see the next items).
  Small airfields and heliports are not candidate airports: their flights
  have no departure or destination airport and no runway events.
- Planned route, planned times and airline schedule are unknown: delays
  against a schedule cannot be computed from OPDI alone.
- A flight split into two tracks gives two rows in the flight list.
- A track with a landing followed at least five minutes later by a take-off
  holds several flights: [0.5 %]{.measured} of the tracks,
  [874 to 937]{.measured} a day. Each flight has its own row
  ([how a track is divided](algorithms/tracks.qmd#flights-of-a-track)). A
  touch-and-go, a go-around and a rejected take-off do not divide a track.
- Placeholder addresses sent by some transponders (`000000`, `000001`,
  `ffffff`) can merge several aircraft into one track, which is not
  flagged.

### Day of a flight

A flight belongs to the day it was first seen, in UTC, with all its events
in that day's files ([Data](data/index.qmd#which-day-a-flight-belongs-to)).

- To count the events or landings that **happened** on a day, read its files
  and the day before's, and filter on `event_time`.
- A flight first seen just before midnight UTC belongs to the earlier day,
  even if it took off after midnight.
- All flights of a track are in the files of the day on which the track was
  first seen, also a flight that started after midnight.

### Reference data

- **Records only in Europe.** The items are compared with the airport
  operator records and Network Manager flight records that EUROCONTROL holds,
  which cover the European area; many airport records are to the whole
  minute ([what OPDI is compared with](accuracy/index.qmd#what-opdi-is-compared-with)).
  Outside Europe only how often an item exists can be measured, not whether
  it is right, and several items have no reference anywhere.
- **Open sources.** Airports and runways come from OurAirports, airport
  layouts and stand names from OpenStreetMap, aircraft registrations, types
  and operators from the OpenSky aircraft database. Their errors and gaps carry over: a runway
  missing from OurAirports gives no runway events; unmapped taxiways, aprons
  and stands give no surface events, block times or stands; a stand drawn
  without a name gives no stand name.

### Position errors and vehicles

- **Spoofing.** Near areas where satellite navigation is disturbed (GPS
  spoofing), positions can jump, or step by 5 to 20 NM and stay. Jumps implying more
  than 1,000 kt are left out of the crossings and the distance flown; a
  spoofed position that does not jump (a frozen position) still misleads the
  detectors.
- **Vehicles.** Airport vehicles and some towed aircraft carry transponders.
  Tracks that never leave the ground and have no aircraft type, or a vehicle
  type, are marked `info.ground_only` on their surface events and get no
  block times; they remain in the flight list.
- **Plausibility checks** remove only events the track clearly contradicts; a
  wrong but plausible event stays.

## Tracks and flight identity {#lim-tracks}

### When it is missing

- A flight that no receiver heard has no track.
- A flight heard in pieces far apart can be split into several tracks: a
  silence over 30 minutes stays inside one track only when both sides look
  like the same flight en route.

### When it can be wrong

- Aircraft merged by a placeholder address
  ([Flights are tracks](#flights-are-tracks)).
- Training circuits with full stops at one airport stay one row: a track
  keeps one take-off and one landing per airport.
- A call sign broadcast wrongly for a long time can split a flight.

### What not to conclude from it

- The number of rows is not the number of flights flown: a flight heard in
  pieces has several rows. Count with the
  [movement columns](algorithms/movements.qmd).
- A `flight_id` ending in `-L<number>` is one flight of a track that holds
  several. To join flights to tracks, remove that ending.
- `flt_id` is the call sign broadcast most often, which may differ from the
  filed flight plan.

## Departure and destination airports {#lim-airports}

### When it is missing

- `adep` is empty when the first report is more than 30 NM from any candidate
  airport or more than 15,000 ft above it (first heard in cruise), and when a
  track first heard in the air descends.
- `ades` is empty when the track ends without descending near a candidate
  airport (reception lost in cruise or far out).
- [24.1 %]{.measured} of the flights had no
  `adep` and [35.6 %]{.measured} no `ades`.
- At a few busy European airports OPDI names the airport as destination of
  only a small share of the recorded arrivals, because the OpenSky data hold
  no reports near the ground there
  ([where no take-off or landing time exists](accuracy/airports.qmd#no-times)).

### When it can be wrong

- At airports close together the nearest airport can be the wrong one,
  though the direction of flight decides between airports less than 2 NM
  apart.

### What not to conclude from it

- An empty airport is not always an overflight: it can be a flight to a small
  airfield, or one whose end was not received.
- `adep_source` and `ades_source` say how sure the answer is;
  `runway_event` is the most reliable.

## Aircraft details {#lim-aircraft}

### When it is missing

- When the address is not in the OpenSky aircraft database of October 2024:
  aircraft registered later, military aircraft and many light aircraft.
- [17.2 %]{.measured} of the flights the
  Network Manager records had no type in OPDI.

### When it can be wrong

- When an address moved to another aircraft after October 2024, or the
  database entry is wrong.

### What not to conclude from it

- `icao_operator` is the aircraft's registered operator, not necessarily the
  airline that flew the flight (wet leases, code shares).

## First seen and last seen {#lim-first-last-seen}

### When it is missing

- The columns are never empty. Every track has one `first_seen` and one `last_seen`
  event: on a track that holds several flights, only the first flight has
  the `first_seen` event and only the last the `last_seen` event.
  A track without any measured position takes them from its measured
  altitude or speed.

### When it can be wrong

- They are exact as reception times, with one exception. For a flight that
  is not the first of its track, `first_seen` is the time at which the track
  was divided, not a report time; the same holds for `last_seen` of a flight
  that is not the last.

### What not to conclude from it

- They are when the aircraft was first and last heard, not its off-block,
  in-block, take-off or landing times.

## Milestone columns and movements {#lim-flight-list-milestones}

### When it is missing

- Empty when its event was not found (see the event's section).
- `aobt`, `aibt` and the stand columns are often empty, because they need
  reception at the stand.

### When it can be wrong

- As wrong as the event behind it.
- A row with no departure (or destination) airport can still have `aobt` and
  `stnd_dep` (or `aibt` and `stnd_arr`) from a block time at a named stand,
  with no airport to check them against.

### What not to conclude from it

- The movement columns (`superseded_*`, `movement_*`) have not been checked
  against official counts; two real short flights of one aircraft within
  3 hours at one airport can be counted as one.

## Take-off and landing times {#lim-take-off-landing}

### When it is missing

When the aircraft was not received near the runway (airports far from any
receiver have few times). Runway-pass times need reports on the runway or
less than 1 NM short of it; runway-window times, within 5 NM and 1,500 ft of
the airport.

- A landing whose reception ends in the flare, before any report on the
  runway, can get no landing time.
- A take-off first received more than 1,500 ft above the track's ground
  altitude at the airport gets no take-off time.
- Some busy European airports have no take-off or landing time at all on the
  three days measured: the OpenSky data hold no reports near the ground there
  ([where no take-off or landing time exists](accuracy/airports.qmd#no-times)).

### When it can be wrong

- Runway-window times (`info.method` = `legacy`) are the first or last report
  of the climb or descent, so less precise:
  [94.3 %]{.measured} of the runway-pass take-off times and
  [91.5 %]{.measured} of the runway-window ones were within 60 s of the
  airport records; for landings, [97.1 %]{.measured} and [87.9 %]{.measured}.
- Where reception starts at lift-off or ends over the threshold, the time
  comes from a report up to 1,500 ft above the ground; `info.at_track_edge`
  marks the track's first or last report.
- At a few airports the runway named, or the take-off time, mostly disagrees
  with the records; at Malta the records disagree with the aircraft's own
  track
  ([where an item is unreliable](accuracy/airports.qmd#unreliable)).
- With no ground report at the airport, height is measured above the
  published elevation, so low or high pressure moves the 15 ft crossing
  (`info.height_reference` = `elevation`).

### What not to conclude from it

- The two methods have different errors: separate them with `info.method`
  when comparing airports.
- A track keeps one `ATOT` and one `ALDT` per airport: a second take-off or
  landing at the same airport is not published, so training circuits with
  full stops at one airport stay one flight.

## Other runway events {#lim-runway}

### When it is missing

- `line-up`, `take-off-roll` and `runway-vacated` need a report on the runway
  itself: where reception starts at lift-off or ends over the threshold, they
  are not published. `line-up` and `take-off-roll` are not given for a
  touch-and-go or a low approach.
- `xing-runway-threshold` needs reports in the last minute before the runway,
  at most 300 ft above the ground there.
- Runway crossings need ground reception on the runway.

### When it can be wrong

- When reception starts during the take-off roll or ends during the landing
  roll, `line-up`, `take-off-roll` and `runway-vacated` mark the first or last
  report received on the runway, which can be at high speed.
- A go-around detector based on heights can count a training low approach,
  and misses go-arounds started above 1,500 ft.

### What not to conclude from it

- No reference gives line-up, take-off roll, runway vacated, go-around or
  runway crossing times: these events are not validated, only compared with
  the recorded take-off or landing.

## Off-block and in-block times {#lim-block-times}

### When it is missing

- Often: they need reception at the stand and on the taxiway, and a stand
  passage in the track. An arrival with no position or speed after the
  landing roll gets no in-block time.
- [35.1 %]{.measured} of the recorded
  off-blocks had an `AOBT` and [33.4 %]{.measured} of the recorded in-blocks
  an `AIBT`.
- **The main limit:** an off-block time needs the aircraft to be received on
  its stand before it leaves. On 14 June 2026 that was so for
  [15 %]{.measured} of the departures in the airport records.
- At [38]{.measured} of the 100 busiest European airports almost no aircraft
  is received on the ground
  ([where ground events are nearly absent](accuracy/airports.qmd#ground-reception)).
- At the airports whose stands are received, [38 %]{.measured} of the
  departures are received before off-block, against [73 %]{.measured} of the
  arrivals after in-block: the transponder is switched on during or after
  push-back.

### When it can be wrong

- When the transponder is switched on during push-back, or the aircraft is
  first received already moving, the off-block time is the first movement
  received: late. A stand with few reports with a position also makes it
  late.
- `info.first_seen_on` says where the aircraft was when first received on the
  ground. Within 60 s of the airport records:
  [67.4 %]{.measured} of the off-block times first seen on a stand (median
  difference [39 s]{.measured}), [63.1 %]{.measured} on an apron
  ([44 s]{.measured}) and [9.6 %]{.measured} on a taxiway
  ([329 s]{.measured}). Leave out the times first seen on a taxiway.
- Off-block times are often late: [48.6 %]{.measured} are within 60 s of the
  airport records, with a median difference of [64 s]{.measured}, and over
  the differences of up to 300 s they are on average [63.9 s]{.measured}
  later. When the aircraft was received at the stand before off-block,
  [78.7 %]{.measured} are within 60 s (median [29 s]{.measured}). In-block
  times are closer: a median of [34 s]{.measured}, and on average
  [18.6 s]{.measured} earlier over the differences of up to 300 s.
- A tow or a change of stand within 10 minutes before the departure is taken
  as the push-back.
- The off-block time is 10 to 20 s after the wheels start to turn.
- Where a stand is drawn inside a larger stand area, the block times read the
  inner one.

### What not to conclude from it

- A missing block time does not mean the aircraft did not park.
- Taxi times from `AOBT` are more often too short than too long, because a
  late `AOBT` is the common error.

## Airport surface events {#lim-surface}

### When it is missing

- At airports without ground reception or without a mapped layout in
  OpenStreetMap. An area mapped without a name gives no `info.osm_ref`.

### When it can be wrong

- Vehicles: see [Position errors and vehicles](#position-errors-and-vehicles).
- An entry at a track's first report or an exit at its last is when
  reception started or stopped (`info.at_track_start`, `info.at_track_end`),
  not a movement.
- Where a stand is drawn inside a larger stand area, both passages are
  published; the larger carries `info.encloses_stand`.

### What not to conclude from it

- A `deicing_pad` event means the pad area was passed, not that the aircraft
  was de-iced.
- `entry-threshold` and `exit-threshold` are aircraft on the ground near the
  threshold markings (lining up), not the landing crossing of the threshold,
  which is `xing-runway-threshold`.

## Vertical profile {#lim-vertical}

### When it is missing

- Level-offs need both tops; tops need altitudes in the air.
- A flight-level crossing needs reports with altitude either side of the
  level within 30 minutes. A flight that levels off at a crossed level has no
  crossing of it.
- No level segment is published on reports flagged on the ground, or less
  than 200 ft above an airport within 10 NM of it.

### When it can be wrong

- A flight without a cruise (short, training) gets its highest report as
  tops; a track holding several flights gets one pair, not one per flight. A top at the edge of
  reception has `info.observed` = false.
- The cruise of light aircraft splits into many level segments and
  level-offs, and the flight phases of slow aircraft are less reliable.
- A crossing between reports far apart in time is an estimate: see
  `info.bracket_s`.

### What not to conclude from it

- None of these events is compared with a reference: no record gives tops,
  level segments or level crossings.

## Distance circles {#lim-rings}

### When it is missing

- When the flight has no departure or destination airport, or reception does
  not cover the circle.

### When it can be wrong

- A crossing across a spoofing step ([Position errors](#position-errors-and-vehicles))
  is kept when it passes one circle only, marked `info.position_jump`; larger
  steps give no crossing.

### What not to conclude from it

- Only the 40 and 100 NM circles are compared with airport records; the
  others are not validated.

## FIR crossings {#lim-fir}

### When it is missing

- Where no position is received (oceans).
- For stays shorter than 60 s in a region, which count as part of the region
  before.

### When it can be wrong

- The boundaries are those of one AIRAC cycle, 524 (28 November to
  26 December 2024), for every day. An **AIRAC cycle** is the 28-day period in
  which changes to aeronautical data, such as airspace boundaries, take
  effect; crossings follow a boundary's old line where it has moved since.
- A crossing placed between two reports far apart in time
  (`info.bracket_s`) is an estimate.

### What not to conclude from it

- A crossing with `info.vertical` = true is a climb or descent between a
  lower and an upper region, not a lateral boundary crossing.

## Holding {#lim-holding}

### When it is missing

- Holds below 2,500 ft above the airport, slower than 140 kt or shorter than
  240 s are not found, nor holds cut by a reception gap.

### When it can be wrong

- Aerial work, survey, firefighting and training flights that circle meet the
  definition; they usually get `info.context` = `other`.

### What not to conclude from it

- Not every hold is arrival delay: use `info.context` = `arrival` for delay
  statistics.

## Point merge {#lim-point-merge}

### When it is missing

- Only arrivals at the airports in the reference table are examined.
- A leg cut by a reception gap, or shorter than 90 s, is missed.

### When it can be wrong

- At airports with several systems close together, a leg can be given to the
  wrong merge point.
- `pms-merge-point` is linked to the runway landed on only where the system's
  name says which runway it serves.

### What not to conclude from it

- `pms-merge-point` with `info.via_leg` false is an arrival that passed the
  merge point without a leg being found, not necessarily one sent direct.

## Measurements {#lim-measurements}

### When it is missing

- `distance_flown_nm` is empty before the first known position, and on
  tracks without any position.
- `time_passed_s` is empty on an event earlier than `first_seen`.

### When it can be wrong

- Across a reception gap the distance adds the straight line, so it is a
  lower bound. Position jumps that imply more than 1,000 kt are not added
  ([Position errors](#position-errors-and-vehicles)).

### What not to conclude from it

- Both count from the start of the track, not from the off-block or the
  take-off: a track first received in the air starts later. On a track that
  holds several flights they count from the start of the track, not of the
  flight. Use differences between two events of the same flight.
